author: Adam
title: My jack plane doesn't work past a certain point
body: I'm using a Stanley jack plane no. 5. I'm not a pro, but I've set it as good as I could. It works nice, takes quite fine shavings, but only until the point when the piece I'm working on is relatively flat. Usually I can see it's going well, when I check it with a straight edge lengthwise I see I'm almost there... and the plane stops taking anything off. When this happens and I try to stick out the blade a little more (I suppose it's not the right thing to do but I have no better ideas), it still won't bite any material, so I try a little more and more, way past a reasonable point, and suddenly it jams because it finally bites in, but the shaving it tries to take off is way too thick. It seems that there's no in-between in this scenario - it either takes off nothing or whole chips. What could be the reason for this and how to fix it? I don't think it's a dull blade, I know how to sharpen it properly. The chipbreaker sits nice on the blade too. Could it be sole not being flat enough? When I check its flatness with a straight edge, the highest points are at the very front and back of the sole, with a tiny gap between these points. I watched some videos on this topic, but my conclusion is that there's no single truth about that in the woodworking world. I'd rather not experiment with flattening the sole unless I've tried other, less invasive solutions, since it's my only plane and right now I can't afford a new one in case I mess up this one. Edit: To clarify, the area around the mouth is slightly below the toe-heel line. I don't have a feeler gauge to check the gap that forms when I check the sole's flatness, but a normal piece of paper wouldn't slide there, while a piece of tracing paper can go through the gap freely. My chipbreaker is about 2 mm from the blade's edge. The situation I'm describing occurs both with pieces shorter and longer than my plane. Here's an example of a shaving I can get when a piece I'm working on is still pretty far from flat. It's thin enough to see through it.

author: Drew
title: How do I fill holes in new pine furniture so that the color will continue to match as the wood ages?
body: I made a pine bookcase about 5 years ago. Initially it was a light blonde color, but it has darkened a lot over time. The problem is I used some wood filler on it, and the wood filler did not darken. Now it stands out like a sore thumb. See photo: I'm not looking to fix it, I'll just live with this one, but is there any way to avoid this in the future? The wood was covered with 2 coats of water based clear polyurethane.

author: Generic_User_ID
title: Bandsaw noise while resawing worries me. Will blade snap?
body: https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/9h849rr5bteuygkyed61y/Video-Dec-16-2025-16-26-09.mov?rlkey=5pqq01a7bl7adj059n76hw6kt&st=a2cr9hev&dl=0 https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/s9bem25ex77mlok7dk26z/Video-Dec-16-2025-15-05-46.mov?rlkey=62b4ahlwnnyovvk0xkqgqzmrg&st=3249bomb&dl=0 The first clip shows me slowly pushing a Southern Yellow Pine 2x8 through a 1” wide Resaw King blade installed on a JET JWBS-18-QT3. The second clip shows the bandsaw running with no wood pushing into it. You can hear the chk-chk-chk sound in the first clip and see in the second clip how the blade goes backwards and forwards by a millimeters. Last time I heard that sound while resawing was on another bandsaw, and the blade on that saw snapped less than one minute later. I’m wondering if only a few of the blade’s teeth are engaging with the wood. I’ve tensioned the blade in this bandsaw according to what I’ve seen in Alex Snodgrass videos. The gullets of the teeth are centered on the crown of the top wheel. When I put the bandsaw in the full tension position, and press hard on the left side of the blade in the top wheel section, it deflects by 1/8” at most. The blade has the same rhythm when resawing even when I set it at a lower tension. I feel resistance when pushing the 2x8, or even a 9” wide Poplar board. This bandsaw has a 3 horsepower motor. Am I doing something wrong? Is it the bandsaw? The blade? Something else?

author: rpspringuel
title: How to deliberately get blade burn?
body: While working with some black cherry that was felled on our property, I noticed that when I got blade burn the wood would turn this lovely shade of purple. I’d now like to draw that color out as a deliberate finish, but I’m having trouble doing so. I tried sweeping a butane torch over the surface, but this tends to draw out more black than purple (in a way that also makes for a nice finish, just not the one I was shooting for). Does anyone have any ideas for how I can draw out the color of the blade burn as a finish on an assembled project?

author: Bman
title: Broken Chair Stretcher/Rail
body: Let me begin by saying I'm not a wood worker, just a guy trying to fix a broken chair. I have a dining chair that has a broken stretcher/rail and I'm struggling with the best way to repair it. The end broke off inside the leg (about 1 inch of wood). The broken off part, of course, needs to be replaced and I think I know the best way to do that but I don't have the tools that I need to do that. I don't have a drill press, table saw or lathe but I have plenty of hand tools. This type thing is not something I do often so I don't want to invest a bunch of money on tools that will seldom be used. On my own and from research I think the best way to fix it is to use a dowel rod of the same size to extend it and use smaller dowel pins to connect the new end to the existing stretcher. I have those things and two problems have come up. The end of the stretcher is 5/8" and I chosen 5/16" dowel pins to connect the two ends. Problems I'm having: Marking the center of the ends for drilling and drilling holes in both ends so that they meet well with dowel pins in them. Without a drill press to accurately drill holes for the dowel pins and some tool to find the center of the two ends to drill I'm kind of at a loss at what to do next. If someone can provide some advice on this it would be much appreciated otherwise the only thing I can think of doing now is to use epoxy to glue a new end to the stretcher and use a long screw to drill through the leg and into the new stretcher end.

author: farazan
title: Can I apply polyurethane on wood treated with osmo polyx and top oil?
body: My kitchen countertops are already treated with osmo polyx and osmo top oil. I want to apply polyurethane to make them more durable to the type of use they are seeing. I have read online in some forums that as long as the osmo has had 3 weeks to cure, it will be fine, but that I may need to apply shellac firs... Is this true? What is the best way to apply polyurethane on a wood treated with osmo?

author: Sketcher
title: How do I prevent wood from vibrating in a "Bladerunner" saw when cutting a curved contour?
body: 2 ][1] 1 I have access to a "Bladerunner" saw. I'm not sure if this would be considered a band saw. When I try to saw a piece of wood along curved contours, the wood vibrates up and down and jumps out of my pencil lines. I've attached a 5 second GIF-formatted video. How can I better control the wood to follow an outline more exactly? Thanks for any info.

author: Simon Tye
title: Epoxy chips when router surfacing an epoxy river table
body: l'm making an epoxy river table using a standard sled on rails setup. Previously I was using a very old ryobi RE120 handy router with a new (but used) 19mm Freud cutter which was cutting well enough , however on the fifth or sixth pass (router not strong enough to cut more that 0.5-1mm at a time) I noticed that the cutter was beginning to dig in. To cut a long story short, I went and bought a Bosch GOF1250Ce router and a new unbranded (well... Aiperq) surfacer bit (dia 39mm) reduced from €40 to €25. Bit seemed ok - edges seemed sharp enough. Router is definitely ok. Table now probably 2 months old whereas it was about 2-4 weeks old when I started flattening it. Did one pass and I noticed where the cutter had passed over the epoxy, it was glittering where the cutter had taken tiny chips out of the epoxy. Also the edge had chipped rather than being a nice crisp 90° edge. Reduced the router speed to minimum but it still chipped. Any advice or ideas, please? Id prefer not to have to buy a branded surfacer bit if I can - I was hoping the difference would be limited to how fast the blades blunted rather than something else. Thanks for any suggestions in advance!

author: ww_init_js
title: Cope-and-stick joint repair -- can pin nail be removed from joint?
body: I am tasked with repairing a cope and stick panel door for a large display case (with multiple such doors). The joints on the frame are starting to come apart due to repeated stress opening and closing. My first instinct would be to take it apart to re-glue it, but the joints are reinforced with a pin nail, and it complicates the process. Can one remove this pin? Here's one of the 4 joints: ( full res1 , full res2 ) As you can see I can crack it open by a few degrees. All four corners have this issue. I just apply a bit of racking pressure and the joint starts to pivot. The glue is no longer effective, and the only thing holding this joint together is the small pin nail which you can see to the right of the screw hole. (the screw hole is for fastening a metal plate that mates with a magnet to keep the door shut) One of the joints has come apart completely, and that is because the wood surrounding the pin has completely given way: ( full res3 ) You can see the pin passing through the groove. The pin does not go through all the way and is not visible from the front . I have access to this one nail, so I might have an easier time For the other ones... How can I go about taking the joint apart with a limited amount of damage? Ideas (maybe some of these are really bad): Don't take it apart, just add another pin nail or dowel. Bore around the nail, pull it out with mini long-nose pliers, and hide the damage behind the metal plate for the magnet. Found an example here in a chair youtube . Drill straight into the nail with a metal bit. I suspect this won't work very well, and it'll dance around the nail.

author: Jake quin
title: Which back piece mounting orientation produces a stronger cabinet?
body: I am a DIY person and my recent project needs me dive into a little bit into woodworking/cabinet making. I need to make some modular cabinets and I have some 18mm laminated plywood from a previous project that I would like to use. My goal is to make some cabinets for my new machines. These machines vibrate quite a bit so I want to make this cabinet as sturdy as it could be. Instead of a typical 3mm sheet for the backing I decided to use the full 18mm instead so I could put some things on the inside and have a solid mounting. When I did the draft on the design I'm stuck on which one is stronger. How do you do the back of the cabinet (for solid sheet)?This question I think is the stuff that only experienced woodworkers/cabinet makers know through experience which I don't have yet. Should I do it like in figure A where the side pieces are going to be attached to the back piece? The screw will be from the back to the front. Or should I do it like in figure B where the back piece is going to be attached to the side pieces? Screws will be on the sides going into the back piece. Would the screwing method matter on a laminated plywood (12 layers): pocket or just straight?

author: Andrew
title: How thick must a wood workbench table top be to hold a 60 lb max bench mounted bike stand?
body: I have a table that my in laws gave me that I keep in my garage as a workbench. It was originally a display table at a Gap store. It's pretty sturdy with a metal frame but the wood is only roughly 3/8 - 1/2 inch thick (don't be fooled by the 2 inch fake siding in the first picture). I am not some master wood worker with tons of super heavy tools but what I would like to do is mount a bike stand to the table. I am however worried the wood is not thick enough for a 30-60 lb bike to sit on an out stretched arm bolted to the table. Maybe this one for reference . Idk if this link will work because it's Amazon but any table.mounted bike rack would be a fine example for the problem. I could probably dance on the table without an issue but I worry the leverage of a bike on a stand would rip or at least warp and maybe splinter the wood. How thick does a workbench need to be to safely hold a typical work bench mounted bike stand with 4 screw holes? If it isn't thick enough, I have some extra 1/16 inch mild steel sheet that I used for a diy project at a maker space around me. I am thinking I could cut it in half to make roughly two 1 foot by 2 foot sheets, drill some holes in those and attach them above and below the tabletop in the spot where I would put the bike stand (image 2 showing the underside of this spot). My thinking here is that this would add more strength to that specific spot and effectively spread out the force put on the table by the weight leveraged bike stand. Am I overthinking this? I have a history of overthinking any necessary engineering in a diy project I take on.

author: jat255
title: Stability and names of two different square box designs
body: I am very novice as it comes to building things with wood, but am trying to make a protective pest cage for some raised beds out of 2x2 lumber. In laying out my cut list, I can think of two different ways to build the boxes with butt joints that will make up the frame. One (shown on the left) has all the boards cut to the same length, and oriented in a "running" or overlapping fashion. The other (on the right) has two longer and two shorter boards. In most of my searching online, the design on the right seems to be more common, but I'm curious of two things: (1) do these two different layouts have specific names, and (2) is there any advantage or disadvantage of either. The joints will be secured with wood glue and screws. The left design feels slightly easier since all the boards will be cut to the same length, but that's a pretty marginal difference.

author: Themis
title: Ryoba versus tenon saw
body: I have a ryoba saw and I am wondering if I should get a tenon saw too. I've cut a few relatively small (~1 in long, ~2 in wide) tenons using the ryoba and it seems to me that with a router plane and a shoulder plane I can fix most sawing issues. Should I consider buying a dedicated tenon saw? I am not worried about the difference between Western vs Japanese style, rather, would it make my work easier/better/more accurate/other advantage for the price?

author: JohnFx
title: What would be a good way to stabilize this slab from bowing?
body: I'm working on a project using the (1" thick) western red cedar slab pictured below mounted to a heavy stump base to make a freestanding live edge hallway clock that will be roughly 6' tall and 1" thick. While the wood was sitting in the shop I did notice some slight bowing so it rocks a little from top to bottom (top being where the red sander is in the photo). It is POSSIBLE (ok maybe likely) that the movement resulted from it getting rained on in the back of the truck from a sudden thunderstorm that popped up while driving it back from the lumber yard. We let it dry out in the shop for a couple of weeks and tried to stabilize it with clamps while it dried out to minimize it and it MOSTLY worked. The current warping is minimal and acceptable for this project. My concern is avoiding more movement in the completed project. If the project stays dry (it's indoor furniture), is it necessary to add some bracing to the back of the piece to inhibit further wood movement? I'd welcome any suggestions on the best way to do this structurally and aesthetically.

author: nitsua60
title: How do I get this wedge+knife out?
body: I got a new (old) jointer, and need to sharpen the knives. Having removed the wedge's screws, the manual next instructs me to get a small screwdriver under the wedge and pop it and the knife up and out of the cutting head. That guy's not moving. Screwdriver, no. Tapping on the screwdriver with a mallet, no. Penetrating oil seems to have done nothing. I trimmed down an extra 1/4" Allen key to slide it in under there as a mini-prybar, and all I'm doing is bending the long arm of the key. Is it time for a torch? What else should I try first? If it is torch-time, can you please briefly walk me through that process, as I've never had to resort to using heat like that.

author: mike rodent
title: How much damage does a concealed nail do to a quality router bit?
body: Non-professional here, taking my first steps with routers. I have never been so terrified of a power tool, and have watched many YT vids about safety protocols. I have also built myself a router table, complete with prominent emergency palm-size stop switch. I would never even think of using my router hand-held. Anyway ... the task I have to perform is to cut grooves in the edges of some solid pine casement sashes (I have a 1930s house in South London). This is to fit weatherstrip, specifically AQ21. I bought a Wealden 3 mm groover bit for this purpose. So a couple of days ago I processed my first sash, i.e. cut the groove, using 2 passes, on all 4 edges. The groove is beautiful and the weatherstrip fits snugly (after 1 coat of primer I think it will be positively tight). But ... in the course of cutting the final edge there was a spark at the start of the cutting process and then at the end. On examination I saw that my groover bit had cut through a nail at each end. I did in fact do the second pass, and got two more sparks. I have a whole house full of sashes to fit with weatherstrip. I've thought about what to do about this, and now intend to buy a device to detect such concealed nails. I'll probably then attempt to "pre-process" these using my utterly brilliant DeWalt oscillating multitool, which is more than capable of cutting through such concealed nails... And kind of intended for this purpose: in any event a replacement multitool cutter blade is far less expensive than a Wealden groover router bit. But I'm interested to know how much damage might have been done to the bit by these two passes using my groover bit. Clearly a router bit is intended specifically to cut through wood. Some woods are also harder than others. And knots are harder than non-knotty wood. Any views?

author: Nicholas
title: Is there a specific type of epoxy that bubbles less?
body: I've been trying to experiment with epoxy, mostly as a thin coating over wood, though I've been interested in trying deeper pours to create epoxy accent pieces. My initial experience is that it's nearly impossible to get even a thin coating to go on without significant roughness or bubbling. I've tried precoating the wood with a thin coat of poly, which helps a lot. I've also tried using my heat gun on a low setting, which I think helps. But there is always still at least a bubble or two per square inch. I'm doing my coatings in a garage that is out of direct sunlight and is about 70F-80F while coating. Temps drop into the 60s eventually, but not until 10+ hours after epoxy application. I've tried using both chip brushes and foam brushes without much difference. I've also had the problem when doing a thin pour over a test mold. I'm using West System 105/205 and am wondering if this is simply a more bubbly epoxy, or if there are other types designed to bubble less. I purchased this epoxy two months ago so it's still good.

author: Oli
title: Replacing my shop vac with my chip extractor
body: I have two separate dust collection systems: A large, calm 2hp chip extractor going through a 4 inch cyclone separator A small, angry 1400W (nearly 2HP?) shop vac, going through a much smaller cyclone separator. I understand the differences between these systems, static pressure vs airflow, and that's the reason why I've ended up here. I have machines that benefit from HVLP (table saw, planers and bandsaw) as well as hand tools that need pressure (sanding, plunge saws, etc). Past the sunk cost, these machines and their separators take up a huge amount of space in my small shop. I'm constantly trying to find a better solution and the one that keeps bubbling back up is removing the vac. Well this week I got to see. The vac has been on site and I couldn't be bothered replacing it with another so hooked the chip extractor up to my plunge saw. It wasn't awful. It wasn't as good, but wasn't awful. The extractor is a beast but with the step down convertors I'm using, just isn't pulling air that hard . With a little extra pressure, this could replace my shop vac. My question is perhaps a little naïve, and super-optimistic, but is there something like a torque multiplier for dust extraction systems? I'd even be happy with in-line pumps that I can hide in the small-bore piping.

author: MaPe
title: How to glue boards without damaging other layers
body: I am repairing an old table lamp stand, which is constructed from glued planks and veneer on top and plywood on the bottom (see the photos of the bottom). The lamp has been stored in a very humid area, as the wood planks due to expansion and contraction are now split and cracked. I have tried glueing it together and fastening with clamps, only to notice that the plywood at the bottom started to crack and form a "tent" (the layers started to overlap). How should I proceed with the repairs? Should I remove the plywood? Maybe fill in the cracks instead?

author: Oli
title: Thread pitch for wooden screws
body: I'm looking for a tap and die set to make wooden screws for toys. We have a few toys already that have ~10tpi course threads and that seems sensible, but I can't translate that into something searchable; something I can buy on (eg) Amazon. I'm not asking for specific product recommendations (though I'll take them) rather for an inkling as to what these jumbo-threaded things are actually called. Everything I search for returns standard machine measures, which are just too fine for wood, IME. And do, I don't have a rotary CnC or machinist lathe with thread-cutting gears.

author: Bennet
title: Does mud stick less to trail running shoes?
body: I am training for a long cross-country run, which starts and ends on tarmac, but goes on rough paths in the middle. I ran some of it today in road shoes, and they got caked in clay-like mud - not just mucky, but literally had an extra 1-inch "sole" of mud. I guess a lot of the route might be similar, and I'm reconsidering my choice of shoes. Would trail running shoes help with this specific problem? I know they offer better grip, but I guess that goes out the window if the mud is so sticky that they replace your sole. And, would such shoes be suitable for the tarmac bits at both ends of the run? I'm experienced in road running, and don't mind being muddy, but I'm new to cross-country running.

author: Eyal
title: Multiday hike in UK with children
body: I very much enjoy mountain hut treks , and since I've had children I've enjoyed doing them as a family . Over the past few years we've done this only in Austria, especially in the Rax region. I'm guessing at this point my children can walk up to about 10km a day for a few days (a year ago they did about 30-something km in five days). I'm familiar with the mountain hut culture and have done trips (without children) in a few European countries, but never in the UK. Are there any recommended trips? Ideally I'd like something that's less than a week and not too far from London - up to a few hours in a train would be best, up to a few hours drive is also acceptable. Although I'd prefer lodging in places that aren't accessible by car, similar to many Austrian mountain huts, this is not an absolute necessary. Staying in some small hotel in a village is fine too. From my initial research I've found The Test Way and The Clarendon Way , but I'd be glad to hear from someone who's actually done something with children. UPDATE: I'm considering doing a part of the Thames Path, specifically the part which starts in Oxford and walking until Wallingford or Dorchester, in 3-5 days. It's not remote, but it feels like it will be a very English experience, and relatively easy logistically.

author: anatolyg
title: Is it common for caves to have less oxygen? What's there instead?
body: The description for a specific cave warns: "You will have funny feeling in the eyes and throat down there. Oxygen concentration was measured to be 17%". Since the regular oxygen concentration is 21%, what could account for the missing 4%? As much carbon dioxide could be deadly; what else? Is it a common enough issue with caves that it could be answered with a high degree of certainty?

author: Enlico
title: What are these small white things I saw ants carrying?
body: Below are two photographs of my finger tip with two white things on it. I took those from some ants. Many many ants were going back and forth holding these in their jaws. What are they? Are the ants preying on some other insect and these are the victims larvae? Or are ants just relocating and bringing their own larvae with them? Of the two things on my finger, I think they are slightly different stages of the same thing, but I'm not sure.

author: Franck Dernoncourt
title: How to swim while carrying fins (i.e., when the fins aren't positioned on my feet)?
body: When swimming long distances, I sometimes want to remove my fins for a few minutes to rest my ankles to prevent tendon injuries , while continuing to swim. However, in some places, e.g. an ocean, I have nowhere to put the fins. How to swim while carrying fins (i.e., when the fins aren't positioned on my feet)? My equipment: Jammer Anti-UV scuba mask, or anti-UV goggles. sometimes: 2-piece (long-sleeve shirt + pants) or 1-piece wetsuit, sometimes referred to as dive skin . sometimes: Swimming socks . sometimes: gloves. sometimes: Diving hood (if not already included in the wetsuit) or swimming cap. sometimes: snorkel barrel (in front or on the side).

author: User1974
title: Make winter tent wood stove fire last all night?
body: Background: I have a 9-ft x 12-ft Trek canvas wall tent . I’ve built a wood base/deck & frame around the tent with a steel roof. And I’ve installed a wood stove with the pipe exiting through the rear wall: RED MOUNTAIN VALLEY Round Wood-Burning Camp Stove . The campsite is located near Bancroft, Ontario, Canada. Drive in or snowmobile in; 2km from main road. When camping in January and February in -15 deg C temps, our -25 deg C sleeping bags are plenty warm without the wood stove. Even still, it is nice to use the wood stove overnight to take the chill off when getting up to urinate or when waking up in the morning. Problem: The firewood is from dead, very dry trees: mostly Eastern White Pine, with some cedar and oak. So the wood burns quickly and doesn't last more than 3 hours. Next year, I want the fires to last longer. What’s the best way to make long-lasting fires in this scenario? Closing the pipe damper most of the way helps, but doesn’t make the fire last all night.

author: User1974
title: Do smelly fire starter cubes attract animals?
body: I keep fire starter cubes year-round in a permanent canvas tent (tent has a separate roof and platform) for emergencies and easy woodstove fire starting in the middle of the night in winter. Location: Bon Echo area, Ontario, Canada ZIP Original Firestarters - Powered with Energy Granules The side of the box says, "First aid treatment: contains kerosene ." The cubes come in plastic wrapping in the box. But even when unopened, they have a strong smell. My assumption is that the smell is from the kerosene mentioned on the box, although I wouldn't know what kerosene smells like. Question: Does the smell of fire starting cubes attract any animals?

author: Kate Gregory
title: Is there a resource to find trails by elevation gain/loss and length?
body: As part of prepping for a trip, I'd like to do some hikes with a specific elevation gain/loss and of particular lengths. It's fairly straightforward to find hikes in an area (I'm looking in Ontario, north of Toronto as far as probably Algonquin) and then to see what their length, gain, and difficulty level are. But if I find one and say "hm, I'd like double that" there doesn't seem to be any approach other than checking all the other trails nearby and seeing what they are. Is there a tool or website I can use?

author: Nij
title: How does a disoriented cavern diver find their way back to a guideline?
body: In a short documentary about the 1973 diving disaster at 'The Shaft' in Mt Gambier, Australia by channel 'Fascinating Horror', a commenter mentions as part of cave diver certification requirements, A cave diving instructor will literally turn off all lights, spin you around to disorient you and you have to find your way back to the guideline as practice. That's something you need to be able to do to get cave diving certified. written by user @Operngeist1 in approximately July-August 2025 Is this an accurate description of at least one requirement, or at least an example of how to meet a particular requirement? Given the likelihood of it occurring, what exactly would such a process for guideline recovery involve? How does the diver re-orient themselves, and identify the correct direction in which to search for the guideline? What equipment is involved or used, and what non-equipment-based techniques are used if this equipment is also broken, malfunctioning, lost, or otherwise not available?

author: Spaetzle
title: Layering Advice for a -30°C Expedition at 77° Latitude
body: I’m preparing for a 5-day cross-country ski expedition in April near 77° latitude. We will be pulling sleds and material, skiing about 4 hours per day, sleeping in tents, and facing temperatures around -30°C to - 40C. I’m confused about the layering system. I know down is great for warmth, but with strong, very cold winds, I’ve heard Gore-Tex is ideal for wind protection. How should I layer everything effectively in these conditions?

author: Marc Le Bihan
title: Beach lifeguard, is it a role that if you take it, it occupies most of your professional time, or is taken often only seasonally?
body: It's a clever choice for teenagers or young adults to start some Surface water rescue learning if they have the ability to do so. Some of them make that choice aside of their school career (in France, for example, attempting the Brevet National de Sécurité et de Sauvetage Aquatique (BNSSA) ). But what about being a Lifeguard (beach or pool), the higher level? Is it still possible to take this role as a secondary one, a seasonally one? Or does it require so much focusing, so much dedication that if you gain it, it's almost exclusively to make it your main professional activity?

author: ab2
title: What is known about how the National Park Service plans to cope with projected large cuts in Park personnel? Or is the planning just beginning?
body: My husband and I backpacked extensively in the back-country of several western National Parks and wilderness areas for nearly 50 years, particularly Yosemite, King's Canyon and Rocky. That era of my life is now over, mainly because of age-related reduced stamina, but my love for these magnificent national treasures remains as strong as ever. Is anything yet known about what services will be hardest hit under the projected cuts in staff, and which are slated to be preserved at close to traditional levels, and to what extent and where daily admissions might be restricted? I remember a season when roadside trash collection in Yosemite suffered because of reduced staff, and hope there are plans to avoid a recurrence. And, for example, do we know if Search and Rescue will be relatively unaffected, or will some remote areas simply be closed? Finally, are volunteer organizations under the aegis of the NPS forming to take up some of the slack, and if so, what is the best way to support their efforts?

author: Bennet
title: Moving overseas with climbing equipment - safe to send via sea freight?
body: TL;DR - will climbing kit get damaged if shipped overseas with standard movers, in cardboard boxes? I am moving overseas over the summer, and I'm figuring out how best to take my climbing kit (ropes, metal stuff like nuts, slings, in quickdraws and loose ones). Ideally, from a logistics point of view, I'd box them up and send with the rest of my stuff via standard international movers. No doubt the boxes will get shaken a bit, but that's fine. However, they will be exposed, maybe, to some heat, rain, maybe salty air. I am moving somewhere hot, so definitely at various points the boxes will be exposed to hot weather. I assume this is, mostly, fine. The kit will be out of sunlight, courtesy of boxes. I wouldn't imagine it would get so hot as to be dangerous. And a little bit of moisture or salt shouldn't kill them - people climb on sea cliffs in Thailand after all. And the kit is rugged enough not to get damaged by a bit of bashing around. But am I missing something? Of course it would suck to find out mid-fall that somehow this ruined my climbing gear! The alternative would be to pack this all into a suitcase and take that with me on the plane, but it will be heavy and bulky, and thus expensive and problematic.

author: El_Muntagnin
title: Is a bear horn as effective as bear spray?
body: In my country, bear spray is illegal to buy and carry. The authorities suggest to tie a small bell to the backpack when hiking in order to make some noise and avoid surprising a bear at close range (which is one of the most frequent reasons for attacks here in the Alps). Honestly, I found it quite upsetting to have a bell continuously jingling since I walk to find some peace and silence. I was wondering about the effectiveness of bear horns like this : does the bear really run away or does it increase the likelihood of an attack by an upset animal?

author: chaun keiffer
title: What are these and can they travel on my clothes and infest a different house?
body: I found these bugs in abundance. I've never seen ticks infest a home like a bed bug before, but they seem to be just like a tick. Besides, ticks are normally harder to kill. These are quite satisfying; when I push my finger on them, they almost remind me of bubble wrap. What exactly are they? They start as little black round things as babies. The one shown will leave behind a good blood spatter once my finger gets it. I have seen them bigger but forgot to take a pic.

author: H. Pauwelyn
title: How did drops appear on the inside of my tent?
body: It was at the end of August that I was on the GR 20 in Corse. I slept inside a tent at an altitude of 1817 meters inside a storm. Outside, there was heavy wind, foggy and cold. While I slept, sometimes some drops would fall. Where did they come from? Before I went to the GR 20, I slept in the rain; then there weren't falling drops.

author: anatolyg
title: Can I rest on sling hung on my ice axe?
body: Suppose I am ice-climbing and I get very tired mid-pitch. The ice is vertical. I get a very good placement on my ice-axe. I could hang a sling on any of the "hooks" my ice-axe has, and then I'd get a great rest position, not even requiring to use feet. Are these hooks designed for this? Are they strong enough? Can I use any of them or should I use both, with a weight-equalizing system? What backup do I need to have if I am going to rest e.g. 2 minutes in such a position? Should I already have an ice-screw placed close by? Is this idea even useful? I've just thought about it after climbing, never used it.

author: Franck Dernoncourt
title: How to fix a slightly deformed snap hook?
body: This snap hook on my backpack got slightly deformed due to excessive weight. How to fix it? The blue arrow points to the deformity; the red arrow points to the consequence of the deformity, namely a slight opening on the hook.

author: User1974
title: Toilet seat positioning on thunder box
body: I've built a thunder box, aka a vault. The toilet seat positioning fits 6ft tall adults, but I suspect it would not fit young kids in the future. In hindsight, I think the seat is too far back. What's the ideal positioning for a toilet seat? As close to the front as possible, to fit the legs of people of all heights? The thunder box has not been used or installed yet, so it can still be modified. It has a garbage bag nailed to the inside front wall, to prevent urine from coming through the slats. I dont have exact measurements right now, since the thunder box is located 3hrs away from home. But for scale, the top of the box is made of three 2"x8" boards at the front, and a 2"x12" board at the back. Edit: I moved the seat all the way forward.

author: Alan B
title: Noticing quite a few dead birds around - possible bird of prey?
body: I'm not sure I ever saw a dead bird on the ground even though I grew up in the countryside, but this year I've noticed various downed blackbirds and pigeons. The latter in a car park beside a ruined castle building which is quite high and overgrown. If there were are birds of prey resident there, would it be a trait that they would attack other birds if they get too close? This is the east coast of Ireland so if I recall correctly, there are some eagles, red kites and various hawks.

author: John Gordon
title: Why turn on the oven at the start of a recipe?
body: I have noticed that many recipes say to turn on the oven as one of the first instructions, even though there may be half an hour or more of preparation before the dish is actually placed in the oven. This seems wasteful to me, and I usually wait to turn on the oven so that it will come up to temperature more or less at the same time the dish is ready to go in. Am I doing it wrong? Is there some actual reasoning for turning on the oven so early? (I'm aware that some people recommend a long preheat for pizza.)

author: Larin Martin
title: Why is my gooseberry jam so stiff?
body: I attempted making jam for the first time, using wild gooseberries and blueberries that I have on my property. My thermometer never showed a temperature higher than 217F, yet my jam is very stiff. It is not as loose as I would like it. I followed directions and did the cold plate trick, which seemed to be accurate. Why is it gelatinous? I didn't use pectin.

author: WoJ
title: What is this glass device I found next to drinking glasses in the south of France
body: I am in the south of France near Avignon. In the house I rented, next to the glasses, there are some glass devices I have never seen before. Below are some pictures, I apologize for the quality because it is not easy to make a photo of a really transparent, round, thin glass thingie This thing is very light and the glass is very thin. It has a flat part which suggests a way to put it. It could have been a candle holder, but the glass is way too thin for that. It is also placed among the wine-drinking glasses, which suggests a voodoo-like activity involving wine or some other alcoholic beverage. EDIT: I will delete this question if this does not end up being related to wine or, generally speaking, drinking. Not related to drinking at all 🤡. Thank you very much for the answers, I unfortunately cannot delete the question because it has been upvoted and has an answer. But again - thank you!

author: T.E.D.
title: Pancakes: Avoiding the "spider batch"
body: This recent HNQ question on pancakes sticking got me wondering if the good people here might be able to help me solve the biggest culinary mystery of my life. I've been cooking pancakes for over 50 years now. For a while when the kids were young (and thus didn't sleep late that day), I used to do it every Saturday morning. That's several thousand pancakes. So I got pretty good at it, or at least very well-practiced. I've solved a lot of pancake-related issues through sheer dumb random experimentation. However, the first batch is still always problematic. Rather than cooking in a nice even pattern, when I flip the first batch, it has always been browned in an odd spiderweb pattern, with what looks almost like bubbles of lighter-browned surface area separated by the browned bits. My kids (funny how kids in a house develop their own culture) grew to call this first batch "the spider batch", and they all refuse to eat it. This means its always the one I am forced to eat (or throw out). Later batches are never like this, being evenly browned. The "spider batch" also has what I'd call a slightly crusty texture that later batches don't. Here's a picture of a plate 3 three completed batches. Typical first batch shown at the top (12:00) of the plate. This shot shows the "spidering" extended a bit into the edges of the later batches, but the spider batch is still instantly recognizable. My method I use is a Calpalhon griddle straddling 2 electric burners, with the big one set on 5(of 10) and the small one on 7. That keeps the whole griddle relatively evenly heated. I pour my pancakes out to about 3.5" in diameter, as I like that size, and it allows me to make batches of 6 on my griddle. I've come to lightly spray the griddle with pan-coat beforehand, and use a paper towel to even it out and dab up any excess. If I don't apply the pan-coat, I often have a lot of trouble with the pancakes sticking and tearing up (but still have a spider-batch issue). If I don't dab it up, the spider batch is much worse, and in extreme cases extends to the second batch. I also allow the griddle to pre-heat for at least 5 minutes, as that seems to help reduce spidering, but it doesn't eliminate it either. I tried looking this up online, and found this thread on the topic on r/Cooking . The advice there seems to be to do exactly what I'm doing with the oil and the paper towel. Its cool that I hit on the same technique everyone there has, but my problem is it doesn't really fix the issue. It alleviates it, but doesn't fix it. The only fix I've ever found is to throw away the 1st batch. Seems like there ought to be a better fix. So the question is, what on earth is causing this spidering, and is there anything I can do to stop it? Or is my current MO of "plan to throw the first batch away" as good as I can get?

author: NjyReading
title: Best method to reheat Tri Tip beef roast?
body: I roasted two tritips at once, each just a bit over 2 lbs. Each roast was taken up to 140°F(max temp) during rest. We only ate one. I want to serve the second one the next day. Can I take the 2nd roast out of refrigerator, let it come towards room temp for an hour, put a probe in it, wrap it in foil, bring right back up to 135°-140°, and serve it? Will that wreck the texture? Is there a better method?

author: IdenticallyEulerian
title: Does the water content inside food regulate the cooking process?
body: I wanted to first start by clarifying that the question I am not asking is the role of using water in cooking e.g. by boiling or steaming as a means of heat transfer. Instead, I was thinking about the fact that when sweat evaporates from our body, it 'carries off' the associated heat with it. I also thought about the fact that at the beginning of cooking onions, I find that they steam quite vigorously for a long time, but once they've stopped the associated browning we love to see begins to occur. When you are frying something in a pan that contains some amount of moisture, is the rate of change of the temperature of the thing you're cooking largely dependent on the moisture content? Does a piece of food with more water in it take longer to get the non-water parts up to a desired temperature because the evaporation of water into steam slows the total process? Does this mean that foods have been dehydrated without heat that affects the composition of the food (e.g. freeze drying) cook faster after drying because they have no water to regulate the process? Better yet in the onion example, does the moisture content literally limit the temperature of the other material through the rate its evaporating until there's not enough water to evaporate and regulate the change? Apologies for the general onslaught of questions, I am looking for a general answer, but hoped that the 'family' of questions I dropped really pinpoints the concept I am trying to ask about. They all ask how much of a role water plays in the amount of time it takes for a certain mixed-media (the other things surrounded by the water in the food) to get up to a desired temperature for a chemical process to occur. When I've tried researching this before, I just get results on the role of water as a conductor, e.g. in steaming, etc.

author: L.Dutch
title: Reason for not using metal spoon in apple sauce
body: The other day I was checking an apple sauce jar at the local supermarket; it's not a product I usually purchase, and was thinking of maybe using it somewhere in my meals. Reading its label I noticed the advice to please scoop it by using a plastic or wooden spoon. (see image below, in Dutch, taken from the internet) What is the reason for not using a metal spoon when scooping the apple sauce?

author: Ellen Burnham
title: Keeping meat frozen outside in 20°F (-7°C) weather
body: We lost power about 49 hours ago, during a big ice storm. We had 2 freezers of meats (hamburger, chicken tenders, chicken breasts, beef roast, stew meat, boneless pork chops, 1 whole turkey). We put them in totes and moved them outside where the temperature is around 20°F (-7°C). All the meat still seems to be frozen. And no end in sight for the power outage. As long as the meat doesn't thaw, will it be okay?

author: brief
title: How to make a sweet with liquid center inside a chocolate or flavored icing?
body: In a restaurant lately I tasted a sweet that had a thin encasing of chocolate or berry/fruit-flavoured icing. The encasing melted quickly in the mouth and the juice was released. How do I make something similar? Is the encasing made around frozen juice? If so, how is melted chocolate to be combined with it? Or any other form of encasing for that matter. How are the sweets served, if they are to be stored in the freezer upon preparation?

author: ConanTheGerbil
title: Why wrap fruitcake in grease-proof paper?
body: Many fruit-cake recipes suggest that to preserve fruit cake it should be wrapped in either grease-proof paper or baking parchment before being placed in a sealed container. Why? I can understand that grease-proof paper might help to keep the air out and the moisture in back in the days when cake tins really were made of tin - and the lid wasn't a very good seal. But is this still needed in the days of close-fitting tupperware (or similar) plastic containers?

author: Ferinix
title: Traditional German recipe involving boiled and fried bread, with seasoned Tuna and Lemon Juice?
body: I'm not sure if dish identification is on-topic with this site, so feel free to correct me if it isn't. I have some older German-descended family members who make a traditional dish I would like to find more information on. The dish itself is pretty basic. A simple egg/flour-based bread dough is flattened, sliced into triangular or freeform pieces, shortly boiled in water, and then fried in oil. The bread can sometimes be salted or contain other seasoning. The bread is served with minced and fried Tuna patties or other Tuna dishes, and is eaten with the fish, often with lemon juice sprinkled onto the bread and fish. Its a dry and savory/sour dish, meant to be shared by a group. Ive also been told it was a dish made during impoverished times. My family members say this dish is called (a word I don't know the spelling of, neither do they) something that sounds like Nymph or Nypp / Nyff (closest German word I can find is Kniff). Its a recipe that has been passed orally through a couple family lines so the actual word may be lost. For the life of me I cannot find information about this dish anywhere on the internet. Ive described the dish, searched dishes made by the locals, searched for dishes prepared in a similar manner, but I can't find anything that matches the description of it. I was curious if any well-known traditional dishes matched or were similar to this.

author: user212290
title: Is the rosemary sprig served with meat edible?
body: After I eat meat, when it is served with a stem of rosemary – with leaves. , I eat that sprig. You can see the rosemary springs below. I've been doing this for my whole life - I'm a senior citizen now. But yesterday, the server suggested that the rosemary was actually not meant to be eaten! Is the rosemary served with meat edible? author: Hollis Hurlbut
title: When making Mole sauce, can I use dried Plantain chips instead of fresh?
body: I've found a Mole recipe that I'd very much like to try. It's by Chef Saúl Montiel and can be found on the Epicurious Youtube channel . The problem is though, one of the ingredients is fresh, ripe Plantains. Which would be very difficult and / or expensive for me to source in my part of the world. So I was wondering whether I could use a bag of Plantain chips instead? Chef Montiel specifies ripe Plantains for their sweetness. I've found Plantain chips that are unflavoured but advertised as being naturally sweet. Given that one of the other ingredients he uses is Vanilla cookies, I'm think using dried Plantain might not be so outlandish but I'd be grateful for some input on the question.

author: Martin Guillot
title: where and when to put a good olive oil in focaccia?
body: I have recently bought a bottle of very good olive oil, and I was wondering whether to put some in my next focaccia. My main interrogation is regarding when I should use it (along a lower quality oil). Should I put it inside the dough so it's protected against the heat of the oven, or just before cooking as to not dilute it with the other oil? Or maybe it would be a waste and I should stick to regular extra virgin olive oil? What do you think?

author: Diane
title: Is it normal to find an egg with 3 yolks?
body: This morning I cracked open a brown egg that was extremely large and there were three (3) yolks inside the egg. Is this rare? Why does a hen lay a 3 yolk egg? By the way, the hen is a Buff Orpington.

author: Victor Feagins
title: Induction Stove How to stop high pitch painful ringing during use?
body: I was at a friend's place and I noticed that when he used his portable induction stove top that it would make a high-pitched noise that most people could not hear but I found to be quite unpleasant. I have only read good things about induction stoves and was quite surprised that they were capable of producing this high pitched noise. Do people have experience with this? What are ways to prevent the high pitched noise from happening? I would like to one day have an induction stove but will not invest if this high pitched noise is an issue.

author: Luke Sawczak
title: Milk well crumbed
body: John Bunyan writes in Pilgrim's Progress, Second Part (1684, England) of a supper at which a curious dish is served: The next was a dish of milk well crumbed. But Gaius said, 'Let the boys have that, that they may grow thereby.' (The remark of Gaius' is no doubt a spiritual point alluding to passages like this .) What was "milk well crumbed"? My grandma suggests that it refer to pieces of bread floating in the milk, like she used to have when she was sick as a child in her Pennsylvania Dutch family, and my mom adduces the word "milktoast" that might refer to the sogginess of the same.

author: Luke Sawczak
title: Can a cake get brownie-like "edges"?
body: In this video about trying to bake a brownie with no "edges" (crusty areas subjected to higher temperatures for longer), there's a moment around 9:40 where the creator's wife asks why cakes don't get those edges. "Now I want a cake with edges," she says. Why can't we have nice things cakes with brownie-like edges? Why do they tend to come out quite uniform in texture?

author: smith
title: Descale a coffee machine and kettle using a generic product
body: For my coffee filter machine the manual does not specify anything about how do descale it. I also have a kettle from the same brand (Russel Hobs in case it matters). I bought a descaler sold by the brand that makes the coffee machine and kettle but the problem is that I cant find it easily/conveniently and it is too expensive. Note that the ingredients they mention on the bottle are citric acid and formic acid. I found in their website that they mention that any descaler or wine vinegar (basically 0.8L vinegar with no water which seems odd) can be used for descaling. My question is: if I buy another descaler that mentions citric acid, should I use the instructions on the package or the instructions mentioned on the descaler of the coffee machine's/kettle brand mentions? UPDATE: I used a citric acid based descaler and tried it with my kettle. I put 50ml of it in 1L of cold water and left it for 90 mins. It did not clean the kettle properly as I see it left residue that does not go away. I don't know if the residue is due the solution not removing the scale completely or from the descaler it self. See photo bellow

author: Stephie
title: Cutting dry lasagna sheets
body: When assembling a lasagna, the sheets will often not fit the pan perfectly. For a large dish, that’s almost a non-issue, because small gaps don’t matter and larger can be filled with bits of a lasagna sheet. It’s ok-ish when the dry sheets shatter a bit. But today I built the lasagna in small individual portions and it was a pain in the proverbial - the sheets were almost impossible to cut or break without shattering. I was working with dry sheets that were quite warped when I took them out of the package. I tried the following: Cut / score with a sharp knife. Unsuccessful, either the whole sheet shattered or it broke off in a random other place. Break by hand. Similar results, it seems the sheets were prone to breaking lengthwise, crosswise resulted in confetti again. In the past, it either didn’t matter or I stored the postage-stamp-sized snippets to be used up in e.g. hearty soups. With a smaller household, I try to reduce such “collections”. My ideal solution would allow me to cut the sheets along a freely chosen line without breakage. I will not switch to sheets that need to be boiled, because that’s a level of hassle that will likely keep me from making lasagna at all.
